turns.reply: Welcome! Today we'll see how components in circuits react to their surroundings, starting with fixed resistors, whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature. What shape of graph does a component like that give when you plot current against potential difference?

Potential difference is the "push" that drives current round a circuit, measured in volts (V). For a fixed resistor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to it. So what shape is the graph of current against potential difference?

Directly proportional just means that if you double the potential difference, the current doubles too. A variable resistor is a resistor whose resistance you can change by hand, by sliding a contact along a resistive track, and it's used in things like volume controls. What is the job of a variable resistor in a circuit?

No problem. Think of a dimmer switch: you slide or turn it by hand, and the light gets brighter or dimmer. A variable resistor works the same way, because sliding its contact changes the resistance, and that changes how much current flows.

If you slide the contact to make the resistance bigger, what happens to the current?

Making the resistance bigger makes the current smaller, because it's harder for current to get through. Resistance is how much a component opposes current flow, measured in ohms (Ω).

What unit is resistance measured in?

Yes, ohms is right. Now a new component: a diode only lets current flow in one direction, called the forward direction.

If you try to push current the other way, what happens to the current in that reverse direction?
recap: Potential difference is the push that drives current round a circuit, in volts.
Directly proportional means doubling the potential difference doubles the current.
A variable resistor's resistance is changed by hand, like a dimmer switch.
Bigger resistance means smaller current, and resistance is measured in ohms.

turns.reply:
Nearly right — it almost stops, because the diode has a very high resistance in reverse, so only a very small current flows, not exactly zero.

Now an LED (light-emitting diode) is a diode that gives out light when current flows through it in the forward direction.

Which direction must current flow for an LED to light up?

LED stands for light-emitting diode. It's just a diode that gives out light when current flows through it the forward way, like in phone screens and traffic lights.

So what does an LED give out when current flows through it forwards?

turns.student: light i guess, anyway im starving
turns.reply:
Yes, light is right, that's what an LED gives out. Sounds like a snack break is coming soon!

Next component: an LDR (light-dependent resistor) is a resistor whose resistance changes with light, and it decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light, what happens to an LDR's resistance?
recap: A diode only lets current flow in one direction, the forward direction.
In reverse, a diode has very high resistance, so only a tiny current flows.
An LED is a light-emitting diode, giving out light when current flows forwards.
LEDs are found in things like phone screens and traffic lights.

turns.reply:
Light intensity just means how bright the light is. A dim room has low light intensity, and bright sunshine has high light intensity.

An LDR's resistance goes down as the light gets brighter. So when bright light shines on an LDR, what happens to its resistance?

Yes — goes down is right, bright light means lower resistance for an LDR.

Next is the thermistor, a resistor that responds to temperature instead of light. The hotter it gets, the lower its resistance. So when a thermistor heats up, what happens to its resistance?
recap: An LDR is a resistor whose resistance changes with light.
Light intensity just means how bright the light is.
Brighter light means the LDR's resistance goes down.
Dim light means the resistance goes up, so it flips the other way.

turns.reply: Yes — "it goes down" is right, a hotter thermistor has lower resistance. That brings us to the end of this lesson. You answered questions on diodes, LDRs and thermistors, and you answered some questions on fixed and variable resistors, where I told you the rest. Go and get that snack, you've earned it!
recap: A thermistor is a resistor that reacts to temperature.
When it gets hotter, its resistance goes down.
An LDR works the same way, but with light instead of heat.
Bright light means lower resistance for an LDR.

turns.reply: Bye, and thanks for working through this today. Come back any time to go over diodes, LDRs and thermistors again, and good luck with the revision!
